title: Thank you, sorry, goodbye
can_do: You can thank, apologise and say goodbye politely.

grammar.heading: Saying thank you
grammar.body: `shukriyaa` is "thank you", and `bahut shukriyaa` is "thank you very much". The usual reply is `koii baat nahiiN`, "no problem" or "you're welcome". These are set phrases, so learn them whole.

grammar.heading: Sorry and excuse me
grammar.body: `maaf kiijiye` means "sorry", and also "excuse me" when you need someone's attention. People often just say `sorry` in the UK, and that's fine with friends and family. With elders and people you don't know, `maaf kiijiye` shows more respect. The answer is the same as for thank you: `koii baat nahiiN`.

grammar.heading: `jii` softens what you say
grammar.body: You've met `jii` as a polite "yes" and after names. Put it in front of these phrases too, and they sound warmer and more respectful. It's optional with friends, and a good habit with elders.

grammar.heading: Saying goodbye
grammar.body: `xudaa haafiz` is the everyday goodbye; many people say `allaah haafiz` instead. Add `phir milenge`, "see you again", and often `inshaallaah`, "God willing". To wish someone well, say `apnaa xayaal rakhiye`, "take care of yourself".

examples.ur: پھر ملیں گے، ان شاء اللہ۔

exercises.prompt: Your neighbour brings round a parcel that was left with them. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: `shukriyaa` is "thank you". Add `bahut` to make it stronger.

exercises.prompt: On a crowded bus, you step on an older woman's foot. What do you say?

options.en: Sorry! Fine as well, in the UK.
No problem. That's what she would say to you.

exercises.explanation: `maaf kiijiye` is the respectful choice with an elder you don't know. `sorry` is fine too, and very common in the UK; it's just more relaxed.
`koii baat nahiiN` is one set phrase: "no problem".
`jii` softens the phrase, and `koii baat nahiiN` stays together in that order.

sentence.ur: پھر ملیں گے، ان شاء اللہ۔

exercises.explanation: `inshaallaah` can go at either end: "see you again, God willing" or "God willing, see you again".

exercises.prompt: You helped your neighbour carry their shopping in, and they say `bahut shukriyaa!` What do you say back?

options.en: Sorry. But you've done nothing wrong.
What's your name? But they've just thanked you.

exercises.explanation: `koii baat nahiiN` is the natural reply to thanks as well as to an apology.

exercises.explanation: `phir milenge` is "see you again", and `inshaallaah` is "God willing".
`jii` at the start is optional and adds warmth. `xudaa haafiz` and `allaah haafiz` both mean "goodbye".

exercises.prompt: Your older neighbour is leaving after a long chat. What's a warm thing to say as they go?

options.en: No problem. They didn't apologise or thank you.
Sorry. There's nothing to apologise for.

exercises.explanation: `apnaa xayaal rakhiye` is "take care of yourself". The `-iye` ending suits an elder.

exercises.en: Goodbye, Aunty. Take care of yourself.

exercises.explanation: `xudaa haafiz` and `allaah haafiz` are both fine for "goodbye", and `aunty` can go at either end.

dialogue.setting: In the car park outside the supermarket, you walk straight into your neighbour Imran and knock his shopping bag. He is older than you, so you call him `imraan saahab`. He's in a hurry.

options.en: Sorry, Mr Imran! Also fine and common in the UK. maaf kiijiye is more respectful.
No problem, Mr Imran! That's what he would say to you.
Thank you, Mr Imran! But you've just walked into him.
